question: Describe a time you had to explain a complex or technical concept to a non-technical audience. How did you approach it?

raiseTranscript.text: I was fixing a caching issue in our app that caused stale data for users. My PM didn't have a tech background so I drew a simple diagram on a whiteboard showing data flowing from DB to cache to user, then explained it like a library book that gets returned to the wrong shelf.
The PM asked questions and we landed on a clearer release note. I asked my mentor later if the analogy worked and adjusted for next time.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: New grad fixing cache bug for PM; used whiteboard + library analogy
Actions: Drew flow, checked understanding mid-explain, sought mentor feedback
Outcome: PM understood release notes; adjusted approach based on feedback
Quote: 'I asked my mentor later if the analogy worked'
Follow-up: How did you know it landed? - 'PM repeated the key point back and stopped asking the same question'
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Candidate described a local scope task of explaining a cache bug using a library analogy after drawing a simple flow. They checked understanding by having the PM restate the point and sought explicit feedback from a mentor on the analogy. This shows coachability and ownership of their own communication. The story stays individual and grounded without claiming broad impact. Biggest strength is the follow-up loop on the analogy; the gap is that the audience was only one person so scope remains narrow.

lowerTranscript.text: I had to explain our API rate limits to the support team. I just sent the technical spec in Slack and they kept asking the same questions so I added more detail from the docs.
Not really, they still escalated tickets to me.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Sent API rate limit spec to support team
Actions: Forwarded technical doc, added more detail when questions continued
Outcome: Team kept escalating instead of handling
Quote: 'I just sent the technical spec in Slack'
Follow-up: How did you check if they understood? - No check described
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Candidate forwarded a technical spec document to support and responded to repeated questions by adding more detail from the same source. No attempt to simplify language, use examples, or confirm understanding was described. The outcome remained unchanged escalations. This shows limited ownership of adapting the message. Biggest gap is absence of any adjustment based on audience signals.

raiseTranscript.text: Sales kept losing deals because prospects didn't understand our new data pipeline latency. I ran a 30-minute session for the sales team using a before-and-after customer story plus a simple timeline graphic. We tracked three deals that month and two closed after the session.
I prepped two non-technical teammates to ask the hardest questions first so I could practice the answers.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Senior explaining data pipeline latency to sales; used customer story + timeline graphic
Actions: Ran session, tracked downstream deal impact, prepped non-tech proxies for Q&A
Outcome: Two of three tracked deals closed
Quote: 'We tracked three deals that month'
Follow-up: What metrics did you use? - 'Closed-won rate on those opportunities'
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Candidate ran a targeted session for the sales team on data pipeline latency using a customer story and timeline graphic, then measured impact on three tracked deals. They influenced without authority by preparing non-technical proxies to test the explanation. Cross-team outcome is visible though modest. Biggest strength is the deliberate practice loop before the session; the gap is that the audience was still within one function.

lowerTranscript.text: I explained our new search ranking algorithm to the marketing team by walking through the code changes in a meeting. They asked fewer questions after I went slower.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Walked marketing through search ranking code changes
Actions: Slowed down the code walkthrough when questions arose
Outcome: Fewer questions but no visible change in marketing work
Quote: 'They asked fewer questions after I went slower'
Follow-up: How did you measure success? - 'Questions went down'
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Candidate presented code changes directly to marketing and measured success only by reduced questions rather than any business outcome. No tailoring of content or follow-up to confirm the explanation drove action. The story lacks cross-team leverage or evidence that the audience could apply the information. Biggest gap is treating fewer questions as the end goal instead of changed behavior.

raiseTranscript.text: Our new infra cost model confused most PMs and caused repeated budget debates. I had my tech leads each explain one component to a paired PM in small groups, then I synthesized the top three trade-offs into a one-page decision framework. PMs started using the framework in planning and reduced escalations by half.
How did you handle the leads who struggled to simplify?
I sat in on two sessions and gave them specific feedback on which examples landed.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Manager coaching leads to explain infra cost model to PMs
Actions: Paired leads with PMs, synthesized into one-page framework, coached leads live
Outcome: Escalations cut in half; PMs adopted framework
Quote: 'I sat in on two sessions and gave them specific feedback'
Follow-up: What was the biggest coaching moment? - 'One lead kept using percentages until we switched to dollar examples'
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate built a repeatable process where tech leads explained components of an infra cost model to PMs, then synthesized the output into a usable one-page framework that cut escalations in half. They developed their team by observing sessions and giving targeted feedback on examples. Leverage comes from scaling the explanation beyond themselves. Biggest strength is the coaching loop; the gap is that the metric is internal process rather than revenue or hiring impact.

lowerTranscript.text: I explained the new cost model in an all-hands and sent the slides afterward. A few PMs still came to me directly so I answered them one by one.
Did the team get better at handling this?
I think so, but I still get a few questions a week.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Manager sent cost model slides after all-hands
Actions: Answered follow-ups individually
Outcome: Questions continued at low volume
Quote: 'I still get a few questions a week'
Follow-up: How did you develop others to own the explanation? - No development described
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. Candidate delivered the cost model explanation themselves in an all-hands and handled remaining questions individually. No evidence of coaching team members or creating reusable materials that reduced their own involvement over time. The outcome shows persistent load rather than leverage. Biggest gap is treating communication as a one-time manager task instead of a team capability.

raiseTranscript.text: The board needed to understand why we were rewriting the core recommendation engine instead of adding features. I framed the decision around three customer retention scenarios with simple expected-value ranges and had the data science lead pre-brief two non-technical board members. The board approved the multi-quarter investment without further debate.
I showed the short-term feature velocity hit explicitly so they could weigh it against the retention curves.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Exec framing recommendation engine rewrite for board
Actions: Used retention scenarios with expected-value ranges, pre-briefed two members, surfaced velocity trade-off
Outcome: Board approved multi-quarter investment in one meeting
Quote: 'I showed the short-term feature velocity hit explicitly'
Follow-up: How did you decide what to simplify? - 'Tested the three scenarios with two non-technical execs first'
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate translated a core engine rewrite into three customer retention scenarios with expected-value ranges for the board and secured approval for a multi-quarter investment. They managed ambiguity by explicitly calling out the feature velocity trade-off and used pre-briefs to reduce meeting risk. Strategic judgment is visible in the framing choice. Biggest strength is the pre-work with board members; the gap is that the story centers on one high-stakes meeting rather than sustained org alignment.

lowerTranscript.text: I presented the recommendation engine rewrite plan to the board using our internal architecture slides. After some discussion they approved the budget.
What did you adjust for the audience?
I added a summary slide at the front.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you explained a complex concept to non-technical audience.
Role: Exec presented architecture slides to board
Actions: Added one summary slide
Outcome: Budget approved after discussion
Quote: 'I added a summary slide at the front'
Follow-up: What trade-offs did you highlight? - None described beyond the summary slide
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Candidate used internal architecture slides for a board-level investment decision and made only a minimal adjustment of adding a summary slide. No evidence of translating technical work into business outcomes or surfacing strategic trade-offs in terms the board could weigh. The outcome appears to have required discussion rather than clear alignment. Biggest gap is treating the board as another internal audience instead of adapting to their decision criteria.

diagnostic.senior: Customer story plus graphic for sales
diagnostic.exec: Retention scenarios with expected value for board

diagnostic.manager: Observed sessions and coached leads live
